questions.question: An electric pump can fill a tank in 6 hours. Due to a leakage in the tank, it takes 7(1/5) hours to fill the tank. How much time will this leak take to empty the full tank if water does not get in or out of the tank through any other point during this period?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Filling time (A) = 6 hours

Net filling time (A − Leak) = 7(1/5) = 36/5 hours

Leak empty time = (Product of times) ÷ (Difference of times)

Leak empty time = (6 × 36/5) ÷ (36/5 − 6) = (216/5) ÷ (6/5) = 36 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 36 hr.**

**__Alternate Method__**

 
 **Person / Pipe** **Time (hr)** **Total Work (LCM)** **Efficiency** 
 Pump (A) 6 36 units 6 
 Pump + Leak (A + L) 36/5 5 

Let the total capacity of the tank be 36 units (LCM of 6 and 36/5).

⇒ Efficiency of Pump (A) = 36 ÷ 6 = 6 units/hr

⇒ Combined Efficiency (A + Leak) = 36 ÷ (36/5) = 5 units/hr

⇒ Efficiency of Leak (L) = (A + L) − A = 5 − 6 = −1 unit/hr

⇒ Time taken by leak to empty = Total Work ÷ Efficiency of Leak

⇒ Time = 36 ÷ 1 = 36 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 36 hr.**

**__Additional Information__**

Pipes & Cisterns Basics

Efficiency of an inlet pipe is taken as positive, while that of an outlet pipe or leak is taken as negative.

Time Calculation Formula

If pipe A fills in 'x' hours and pipe B empties in 'y' hours (y > x), then net filling time = (xy) ÷ (y − x).

Total Work Assumption

Always take the LCM of individual time durations to represent the total capacity of the tank for easier calculations.</p

questions.question: A and B complete a work in 6 days. If A alone can do it in 7 days, then B alone can do it in ______________ days.
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__
Time taken by **B** = (**Product** of days) ÷ (**Difference** of days)

⇒ Time = (7 × 6) ÷ (7 − 6)

⇒ Time = 42 ÷ 1 = 42 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 42 days.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Time taken by (**A + B**) = 6 days

Time taken by **A** alone = 7 days

**Method:** LCM Method (Total Work ÷ Efficiency)
 
 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 **A + B** 6 42 7 
 **A** 7 6 
⇒ **Efficiency** of (A + B) = 7 units/day

⇒ **Efficiency** of A = 6 units/day

⇒ **Efficiency** of B = Efficiency of (A + B) − Efficiency of A

⇒ **Efficiency** of B = 7 − 6 = 1 unit/day

⇒ **Time taken by B** = Total Work ÷ Efficiency of B

⇒ **Time** = 42 ÷ 1 = 42 days

**∴ The correct answer is 42 days.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Work and Efficiency Relation

Efficiency is **inversely proportional** to the time taken to complete a work. Formula: **Work = Efficiency × Time**.

Combined Work Formula

If two individuals complete a work in x and y days respectively, their combined time is **(x × y) ÷ (x + y)**.

Pipes and Cisterns

This logic is similar to **inlet and outlet pipes**, where efficiency is added or subtracted based on the nature of the work.</p

questions.question: 3 men and 14 women can complete a piece of work in 18 days, and 11 men and 8 women can complete the same work in 12 days. The work of how many women is equivalent to that of one man?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__
Equate **Total Work**: (3M + 14W) × 18 = (11M + 8W) × 12

Divide both sides by 6: (3M + 14W) × 3 = (11M + 8W) × 2

9M + 42W = 22M + 16W

26W = 13M ⇒ 2W = 1M

**∴ The correct answer is 2.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Case 1: **3 Men** and **14 Women** in **18 days**.

Case 2: **11 Men** and **8 Women** in **12 days**.

**Formula Used:**

Total Work = (Number of workers × Time taken)

**Calculations:**

⇒ Total Work = (3M + 14W) × 18 --- (i)

⇒ Total Work = (11M + 8W) × 12 --- (ii)

⇒ (3M + 14W) × 18 = (11M + 8W) × 12

⇒ 3(3M + 14W) = 2(11M + 8W)

⇒ 9M + 42W = 22M + 16W

⇒ 42W − 16W = 22M − 9M

⇒ 26W = 13M

⇒ 1M = 2W

**∴ The correct answer is 2.**

**__Additional Information__**

Man-Day Concept

Total work is constant and expressed as the product of efficiency and time. M₁D₁ = M₂D₂.

Work and Wages

Wages are distributed based on the ratio of work done, which is often the ratio of efficiencies when time is constant.</p

questions.question: A and B can do a piece of work in 13 days and 52 days, respectively. Both work for 2 days and then A goes away. How long (in days) will B take to complete the remaining work?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Total Work = LCM(13, 52) = 52 units.

Efficiency of **A** = 4 units/day, Efficiency of **B** = 1 unit/day.

Work done in 2 days = (4 + 1) × 2 = 10 units.

Remaining work = 52 − 10 = 42 units.

Time taken by **B** for remaining work = 42 ÷ 1 = 42 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 42 days.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

⇒ Total efficiency of (**A** + **B**) = 4 + 1 = 5 units/day.

⇒ Work completed in 2 days = 5 × 2 = 10 units.

⇒ Remaining work = 52 − 10 = 42 units.

⇒ Time taken by **B** to complete remaining work = Remaining Work ÷ Efficiency of **B**

Work and Efficiency

Work and Wages

questions.question: Jitesh and Kamal can complete a certain piece of work in 5 and 18 days, respectively, They started to work together, and after 3 days, Kamal left. In how many days will Jitesh complete the remaining work?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__
Total work (LCM of 5 and 18) = 90 units.

Efficiency: **Jitesh** = 18 units/day, **Kamal** = 5 units/day.

Combined work in 3 days = 3 × (18 + 5) = 69 units.

Remaining work = 90 − 69 = 21 units.

Days for Jitesh to finish = 21 ÷ 18 = 7/6 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 7/6 days.**

**__Alternate Method__**

 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency**
 **Jitesh** 5 90 18
 **Kamal** 18 5
Given: **Jitesh** completes work in 5 days, **Kamal** in 18 days.

Formula: **Remaining Work** = **Total Work** − **Work Done**

⇒ Total work = LCM(5, 18) = 90 units

⇒ Efficiency of **Jitesh** = 90 ÷ 5 = 18 units/day

⇒ Efficiency of **Kamal** = 90 ÷ 18 = 5 units/day

⇒ Work done together in 3 days = 3 × (18 + 5) = 3 × 23 = 69 units

⇒ Remaining work = 90 − 69 = 21 units

⇒ Time taken by **Jitesh** to finish remaining work = 21 ÷ 18

⇒ Time = 7/6 days

**∴ The correct answer is 7/6 days.**

**__Additional Information__**

Efficiency and Time Relation

Efficiency is inversely proportional to the time taken to complete the work. Efficiency × Time = Total Work.

Work & Wages

Wages are distributed based on the ratio of work done by each individual, which is the product of their efficiency and time spent working.

Fractional Work Method

If a person does work in 'x' days, work done in 1 day = 1/x. Sum of daily fractions of work gives the total combined efficiency.</p

questions.question: A and B complete a work in 14 days. If A alone can do it in 63 days, then B alone can do it half of the same work in ______________ days.
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Time taken by **B** to complete **full work** = (**A × Total**) ÷ (**A − Total**)

⇒ (63 × 14) ÷ (63 − 14) = (63 × 14) ÷ 49 = 18 days.

Time taken for **half of the work** = 18 ÷ 2 = 9 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 9 days.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Time taken by (**A + B**) = 14 days

Time taken by **A** alone = 63 days

 **Person**
 **Days**
 **Total Work**
 **Efficiency**

 **A + B**

 **A**

 2

**Calculations:**

⇒ Efficiency of **B** = (Efficiency of **A + B**) − (Efficiency of **A**)

⇒ Efficiency of **B** = 9 − 2 = 7 units/day

⇒ **Half of the work** = 126 ÷ 2 = 63 units

⇒ Time taken by **B** for half work = 63 ÷ 7 = 9 days

**∴ The correct answer is 9 days.**

**__Additional Information__**

Work and Efficiency Relationship

Total Work = Time × Efficiency. Efficiency is inversely proportional to the time taken to complete the work.

Work & Wages

Wages are distributed in the ratio of the work done, which is usually the ratio of efficiencies if all persons work for the same duration.

Pipes & Cisterns

This concept follows the same logic as Time and Work, where filling is positive work and leakage/emptying is negative work.</p

questions.question: An electric pump can fill a tank in 8 hours. Due to a leakage in the tank, it takes 9(1/3)​ hours to fill the tank. How much time will this leak take to empty the full tank if water does not get in or out of the tank through any other point during this period?

[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Time for pump (A) = 8 hr

Time for pump + leak (A − B) = 28/3 hr

Total Capacity (LCM of 8, 28) = 56 units

Efficiency of Leak (B) = (56 ÷ 8) − (56 ÷ (28/3)) = 7 − 6 = 1 unit/hr

Time for Leak to empty = 56 ÷ 1 = 56 hr

**∴ The correct answer is 56 hr.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Filling time of **Electric Pump** (P) = 8 hours

Filling time with **Leakage** (P + L) = 9(1/3) hours = 28/3 hours

**Formula Used:**

Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time

Time = Total Work ÷ Efficiency

 **Component**
 **Time (hr)**
 **Total Capacity**
 **Efficiency**

 7

 Pump + Leak (P + L)

**Calculations:**

⇒ Efficiency of Pump (P) = 56 ÷ 8 = 7 units/hr

⇒ Efficiency of (Pump + Leak) = 56 ÷ (28/3) = (56 × 3) ÷ 28 = 2 × 3 = 6 units/hr

⇒ Efficiency of Leak (L) = Efficiency of (P + L) − Efficiency of P

⇒ Efficiency of Leak (L) = 6 − 7 = −1 unit/hr (Negative sign denotes emptying)

⇒ Time taken by Leak to empty the tank = Total Capacity ÷ |Efficiency of Leak|

⇒ Time = 56 ÷ 1 = 56 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 56 hr.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Pipes and Cisterns Concept

Filling pipes have positive efficiency, while leakage or outlet pipes have negative efficiency.

Leakage Formula

If a pipe fills a tank in 'x' hours and with a leak it takes 'y' hours, the leak empties it in (xy) ÷ (y − x) hours.

Total Work (Capacity)

LCM of individual time durations is the most efficient way to assume the total capacity of the tank.</p

questions.question: A and B complete a work in 14 days. If A alone can do it in 56 days, then B alone can do three-fourth of the same work in days.
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Combined efficiency (A+B) = Total Work ÷ Days = 56 ÷ 14 = 4

A efficiency = 56 ÷ 56 = 1

B efficiency = 4 − 1 = 3

Time for B to do 3/4 work = (3/4 × 56) ÷ 3 = 42 ÷ 3 = 14 days

**∴ The correct answer is 14 days.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Time taken by (A+B) = 14 days, Time taken by A = 56 days.

**Formula:** 1/B = 1/(A+B) − 1/A

⇒ Efficiency of B = Efficiency of (A + B) − Efficiency of A

⇒ Efficiency of B = 4 − 1 = 3 units/day

⇒ Total Work = 56 units

⇒ 3/4 of Total Work = 56 × (3/4) = 42 units

⇒ Time taken by B = 42 ÷ 3 = 14 days

**∴ The correct answer is 14 days.**

Time and Efficiency Relationship

Time taken is inversely proportional to efficiency. Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time.

Combined Work Formula

If two people work together, their combined efficiency is the sum of their individual efficiencies.

Fractional Work

questions.question: A water tank can be filled in 19 minutes by using 39 pipes of the same capacity . In how many minutes (rounded off to two decimal places) will the water tank be filled if we use 23 pipes of the same capacity as above?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__
Apply the **Inverse Proportion** rule: **M₁ × T₁ = M₂ × T₂**

Where **M** is the number of **pipes** and **T** is the **time** taken.

39 × 19 = 23 × T₂

T₂ = 741 ÷ 23 ≈ 32.22

**∴ The correct answer is 32.22 minutes.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Initial number of pipes (P₁) = **39 pipes**

Initial time taken (T₁) = **19 minutes**

Final number of pipes (P₂) = **23 pipes**

**Formula Used:**

Total Work = Number of Pipes × Time taken

**Calculations:**

⇒ Total Capacity of Tank = 39 × 19 = **741 units**

⇒ Required Time (T₂) = Total Capacity ÷ Number of Pipes

⇒ T₂ = 741 ÷ 23

⇒ T₂ = 32.21739...

⇒ T₂ ≈ **32.22 minutes** (rounded off to two decimal places)

**∴ The correct answer is 32.22 minutes.**

**__Additional Information__**

Inverse Variation in Work

When the **efficiency** of each unit is constant, the time required is **inversely proportional** to the number of units (pipes/men). If pipes decrease, time increases.

Chain Rule Formula

The general relation is M₁D₁H₁/W₁ = M₂D₂H₂/W₂, where M is power, D/H is time, and W is work.</p

questions.question: A and B complete a work in 18 days. If A alone can do it in 24 days, then B alone can do one-fourth of the same work in_______ days.
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Efficiency of **B** = 1/18 − 1/24 = (4 − 3)/72 = 1/72

Time for **B** to do **Full Work** = 72 days

Time for **B** to do **1/4th Work** = 72 ÷ 4 = 18 days

**∴ The correct answer is 18 days.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Time taken by **(A + B)** = 18 days, Time taken by **A** = 24 days.

**Formula Used:** Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time; Time = Work ÷ Efficiency

 
 **Person** **Days** **Total Work (LCM)** **Efficiency** 
 A + B 18 72 4 
 A 24 3 

⇒ Efficiency of **B** = Efficiency of **(A + B)** − Efficiency of **A**

⇒ Efficiency of **B** = 4 − 3 = 1 unit/day

⇒ **One-fourth** of Total Work = 72 ÷ 4 = 18 units

⇒ Time taken by **B** for 1/4th work = 18 ÷ 1 = 18 days

**∴ The correct answer is 18 days.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Total Work Formula

If two people work together, their combined efficiency is the sum of their individual efficiencies: Eₜₒₜₐₗ = E₁ + E₂.

Work and Time Relation

Time is **inversely proportional** to efficiency for a constant amount of work. Work = Time × Efficiency.</p

questions.question: A pipe can fill a tank in 12 hours. Another pipe can empty the filled tank in 14 hours. If both the pipes are opened simultaneously, then the time (in hours) in which the tank will be filled is:
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Net filling time = (x × y) ÷ (y − x)

Here, filling pipe time x = 12 hours and emptying pipe time y = 14 hours.

Time taken = (12 × 14) ÷ (14 − 12) = 168 ÷ 2 = 84 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 84 hours.**

**__Alternate Method__**

 **Pipe Type**
 **Time (Hours)**
 **Total Capacity (LCM)**
 **Efficiency**

 **Filling Pipe (A)**
 12
 84 units
 +7

 **Emptying Pipe (B)**
 14
 −6

**Given:** Filling time = 12 hours, Emptying time = 14 hours.

**Formula Used:** Time = Total Capacity ÷ Net Efficiency

⇒ LCM of 12 and 14 = 84 units (Total Capacity)

⇒ Efficiency of Pipe A = 84 ÷ 12 = +7 units/hr

⇒ Efficiency of Pipe B = 84 ÷ 14 = −6 units/hr (negative because it empties)

⇒ Net efficiency when both pipes are open = 7 − 6 = 1 unit/hr

⇒ Time required to fill the tank = 84 ÷ 1 = 84 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 84 hours.**

**__Additional Information__**

Net Work Done

When one pipe fills (rate x) and another empties (rate y), the net work per hour is (1/x − 1/y). If the result is positive, the tank fills.

Pipes and Cisterns Convention

Inlet pipes are assigned positive efficiency, while outlet (leakage) pipes are assigned negative efficiency.

LCM Method

Total capacity is assumed as the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of individual times to simplify efficiency calculations into integers.</p

questions.question: An electric pump can fill a tank in 6 hours. Due to a leakage in the tank, it takes 7(1/3) hours to fill the tank. How much time will this leak take to empty the full tank if water does not get in or out of the tank through any other point during this period?"

Emptying time = (Product of times) ÷ (Difference of times)

Emptying time = (6 × 22/3) ÷ (22/3 − 6)

Emptying time = 44 ÷ (4/3) = 44 × 3/4 = 33 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 33 hr.**

 **Pipe/Leak** **Time (hr)** **Total Work (L)** **Efficiency (L/hr)**

 **Pump + Leak (A+L)** 22/3 9 

⇒ Efficiency of **Pump** (A) = 11 units/hr

⇒ Efficiency of **Pump + Leak** (A+L) = 9 units/hr

Pipes and Cisterns Basics

Inlet pipes have positive efficiency, while **leakage** or outlet pipes have negative efficiency.

Total Work Calculation

When handling fractions like 22/3 and 6, take the **LCM of the numerators** (LCM of 22 and 6 is 66) to find the total capacity.

Time, Work, and Efficiency

questions.question: An electric pump can fill a tank in 6 hours. Due to a leakage in the tank, it takes 7½ hours to fill the tank. How much time will this leak take to empty the full tank if water does not get in or out of the tank through any other point during this period?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Time taken by **Pump** (A) = 6 hours

Time taken by **Pump + Leak** (A + B) = 7.5 hours

Emptying time for **Leak** = (XY) ÷ (Y − X)

⇒ (6 × 7.5) ÷ (7.5 − 6) = 45 ÷ 1.5 = 30 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 30 hr.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Filling time = 6 hr, Filling with leak = 7.5 (15/2) hr.

**Formula Used:** Total Work = LCM of time; Efficiency = Work ÷ Time.

 
 **Person/Pipe** **Time (hr)** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 Pump (A) 6 30 5 
 Pump + Leak (A+B) 15/2 4 

⇒ Efficiency of **Pump** (A) = 5 units/hr

⇒ Efficiency of **Pump + Leak** (A + B) = 4 units/hr

⇒ Efficiency of **Leak** (B) = 4 − 5 = −1 unit/hr (negative sign denotes emptying)

⇒ Time taken by **Leak** to empty the tank = Total Work ÷ Efficiency of B

⇒ 30 ÷ 1 = 30 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 30 hr.**

**__Additional Information__**

Pipes and Cisterns Concept

Efficiency of an **inlet pipe** is taken as positive, while the efficiency of an **outlet pipe (leak)** is taken as negative.

Net Efficiency

If two pipes A and B work together, net efficiency = Efficiency of A + Efficiency of B. Total time = Total Work ÷ Net Efficiency.

Work-Time Relation

Time taken to complete a task is **inversely proportional** to the efficiency of the worker or pipe.</p

questions.question: A and B complete a work in 15 days. If A alone can do it in 17 days, then B alone can do two-third of the same work in _______ days.
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Combined efficiency of **A + B** = 1/15

Efficiency of **A** = 1/17

Efficiency of **B** = 1/15 − 1/17 = 2/255

Time for **B** to do 2/3 work = (2/3) ÷ (2/255) = (2/3) × (255/2) = 85 days

**∴ The correct answer is 85 days.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Time taken by (A+B) = 15 days, Time taken by A = 17 days.

**Formula Used:** Total Work = LCM of days; Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Days

 
 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 **A + B** 15 255 17 
 **A** 17 15 

⇒ Efficiency of **B** = Efficiency of (A+B) − Efficiency of A

⇒ Efficiency of **B** = 17 − 15 = 2 units/day

⇒ **Two-third** of the total work = 2/3 × 255 = 170 units

⇒ Time taken by **B** alone = 170 ÷ 2 = 85 days

**∴ The correct answer is 85 days.**

**__Additional Information__**

Work and Efficiency Relationship

Efficiency is inversely proportional to the time taken to complete a task. Efficiency = Work ÷ Time.

Fractional Work

To find the time for a fraction of work, multiply the total time required for the full work by that fraction: Timeₚₐᵣₜ = Fraction × Total Time.

Pipes and Cisterns

This concept follows the same logic as Time and Work, where filling pipes have positive efficiency and outlet pipes have negative efficiency.</p

questions.question: A booster pump can be used for filling as well as for emptying a tank. The capacity of the tank is 1800 m³. The emptying capacity of the tank is 10 m³/min higher than its filling capacity, and the pump needs 6 minutes lesser to empty the tank than it needs to fill it. What is the filling capacity of the pump in m³/min?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__
Let **filling capacity** be x. Then **emptying capacity** is x + 10.

Time difference formula: [Capacity / (Smaller Rate)] − [Capacity / (Larger Rate)] = Time Difference

1800/x − 1800/(x + 10) = 6

Test Option (3): x = 50 ⇒ 1800/50 − 1800/60 = 36 − 30 = 6 minutes. Matches exactly.

**∴ The correct answer is 50 m³/min.**

**__Alternate Method__**
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/873b037846b0acb706861f41d7c3360c250ac27e99926814a53490e88414dabc.png] 
**Given:** Total Tank Capacity = **1800 m³**, Difference in capacity = **10 m³/min**, Difference in time = **6 minutes**.

**Formula Used:** Time = Capacity ÷ Rate

⇒ Let Filling Capacity = x m³/min

⇒ Emptying Capacity = (x + 10) m³/min

⇒ 1800/x − 1800/(x + 10) = 6

⇒ 1800 [(x + 10 − x) / (x(x + 10))] = 6

⇒ 1800 × 10 / (x² + 10x) = 6

⇒ 3000 = x² + 10x

⇒ x² + 10x − 3000 = 0

⇒ (x + 60)(x − 50) = 0

⇒ Since capacity cannot be negative, x = 50 m³/min.

**∴ The correct answer is 50 m³/min.**

**__Additional Information__**

Time and Work Relation

Rate of work is inversely proportional to the time taken. If capacity increases, time decreases: Time = Work / Rate.

Quadratic Shortcut

For the equation x² + (a−b)x − ab = 0, the roots are b and −a. In physical problems like capacity, always pick the positive root.

Pipes and Cisterns

Filling is considered positive work while emptying is considered negative work in net efficiency problems.</p

questions.question: Two taps can fill a cistern in 3 hours and 36 hours, respectively. A third tap can empty it in 4 hours. How long (in hours) will it take to fill two-third of the empty cistern, if all of them are opened together?

Combined efficiency = 12 + 1 − 9 = 4 units/hour (Total Work = 36 units).

Work to be done = 2/3 × 36 = 24 units.

Time required = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 6 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Filling Tap 1 (A) = 3 hours, Filling Tap 2 (B) = 36 hours, Emptying Tap 3 (C) = 4 hours.

**Formula Used:** Total Work = LCM of individual times; Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time.

⇒ Net efficiency of all taps = 12 + 1 − 9 = 4 units/hour.

⇒ Target capacity to fill = 2/3 × Total Work = 2/3 × 36 = 24 units.

⇒ Time taken = Target Capacity ÷ Net Efficiency

⇒ Time taken = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours.

Inlet and Outlet Taps

Inlet taps perform **positive work** (filling), while outlet/leakage taps perform **negative work** (emptying) relative to the cistern capacity.

Work and Time Relation

Time is **inversely proportional** to efficiency. If a tap fills a tank in 'x' hours, its 1-hour work is 1/x of the total capacity.

Net Efficiency Formula

For two inlets (a, b) and one outlet (c), the net work done in one hour is (1/a + 1/b − 1/c).</p

questions.question: Three water pipes m, n and p, take 5, 6 and 12 hours, respectively, to fill a water tank. If all three pipes are opened at the same time, then the required time to fill the water tank will be:

**Total Work** = LCM of 5, 6, and 12 = 60 units.

**Efficiencies**: m = 12, n = 10, p = 5.

**Combined Efficiency** = 12 + 10 + 5 = 27 units/hr.

**Time required** = 60 ÷ 27 = 20 ÷ 9 = 2 2/9 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 2 2/9 hr.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Pipe m = 5 hr, Pipe n = 6 hr, Pipe p = 12 hr.

**Formula Used:** Total Work = Time × Efficiency

 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency**
 **m** 5 60 12
 **n** 6 10
 **p** 12 5
**Calculations:**

⇒ Total Efficiency of **(m + n + p)** = 12 + 10 + 5 = 27 units/hr

⇒ Total Time Taken = Total Work ÷ Total Efficiency

⇒ Time = 60 ÷ 27

⇒ Time = 20 ÷ 9

⇒ Time = 2 2/9 hours

**Combined Work Formula**

**Pipes and Cisterns Rule**

**Alternate Filling**

If pipes operate on alternate hours, calculate the work done in one **cycle** (sum of their efficiencies) and then find the total cycles.</p

questions.question: A and B complete a work in 20 days. If A alone can do it in 45 days, then B alone can do one-third of the same work in _______ days.
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Work rate of **B** = (1/20) − (1/45) = (9 − 4) / 180 = 5 / 180 = 1 / 36.

Total time for **B** alone = 36 days.

Time for 1/3 of the work = 36 × (1/3) = 12 days.

**∴ The correct answer is 12 days.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Time taken by **A + B** = 20 days

Time taken by **A** alone = 45 days

**Formula Used:**

Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time

 
 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 **A + B** 20 180 9 
 **A** 45 4 

**Calculations:**

⇒ Efficiency of **B** = Efficiency of (A + B) − Efficiency of A

⇒ Efficiency of **B** = 9 − 4 = 5 units/day

⇒ Total work to be done by **B** = 1/3 × 180 = 60 units

⇒ Time taken by **B** = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 days

**∴ The correct answer is 12 days.**

**__Additional Information__**

Pipes & Cisterns Relation

The concept of Time and Work is identical to filling a tank. If two pipes fill a tank in T days and one fills in T₁, the other takes (T × T₁) ÷ (T₁ − T) days.

Work & Wages

Wages are distributed in the direct **ratio of the efficiency** of the workers or the ratio of work done.

Alternate Day Work

In alternate day problems, calculate work done in a **2-day cycle** first, then multiply to reach near the total work.</p

questions.question: An electric pump can fill a tank in 4 hours. Due to a leakage in the tank, it takes 9 (1)/(3) hours to fill the tank. How much time will this leak take to empty the full tank if water does not get in or out of the tank through any other point during this period?
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Filling rate with **pump** alone = 1/4 tank/hr.

Filling rate with **leakage** (9 1/3 hr = 28/3 hr) = 3/28 tank/hr.

Rate of **leakage** = 1/4 − 3/28 = (7 − 3)/28 = 4/28 = 1/7 tank/hr.

**Time** taken by leak to empty = 1 ÷ (1/7) = 7 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 7 hr.**

**__Alternate Method__**

 **Component**
 **Time (hr)**

 **Efficiency**

 **Pump (P)**

 **Pump + Leak (P−L)**

**Given:** Filling time = 4 hr, Combined time with leak = 28/3 hr.

**Formula Used:** Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time; Leak Efficiency = P − (P−L).

⇒ Efficiency of **Pump (P)** = 28 ÷ 4 = 7 units/hr.

⇒ Efficiency of **Pump − Leak (P−L)** = 28 ÷ (28/3) = 3 units/hr.

⇒ Efficiency of **Leak (L)** = 7 − 3 = 4 units/hr.

⇒ Time taken by **Leak** to empty = 28 ÷ 4 = 7 hr.

**∴ The correct answer is 7 hr.**

**__Additional Information__**

Inlet and Outlet Pipes

An **inlet pipe** fills a tank (positive work) while an **outlet pipe** or **leakage** empties it (negative work).

Combined Efficiency

If pipe A fills in 'x' hours and leak B empties in 'y' hours, net work per hour = 1/x − 1/y.

Emptying Time Formula

If a tank fills in 'a' hours and with a leak in 'b' hours, the leak empties the full tank in (a × b) ÷ (b − a) hours.</p

questions.question: A pipe can fill a tank in 27 hours. Another pipe can empty the filled tank in 28 hours. If both the pipes are opened simultaneously, then the time (in hours) in which the tank will be one-fourth filled, is:

Time to fill full tank = 27 × 28 = 756 hours.

Time to fill 1/4th tank = 756 ÷ 4 = 189 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 189 hours.**

⇒ **Total Capacity** of tank = LCM of 27 and 28 = 756 units.

⇒ Efficiency of **Pipe A** = 756 ÷ 27 = +28 units/hr.

⇒ Efficiency of **Pipe B** = 756 ÷ 28 = −27 units/hr.

Inlet and Outlet Pipes

Inlet pipe efficiency is taken as **positive (+)** and outlet (emptying) pipe efficiency is taken as **negative (−)**.

Net Time Formula

If an inlet fills in 'x' hours and outlet empties in 'y' hours, net time to fill is **(xy) ÷ (y − x)**, provided y > x.</p

questions.question: A pipe can fill a tank in 12 hours. Another pipe can empty the filled tank in 21 hours. If both the pipes are opened simultaneously, then the time (in hours) in which the tank will be half filled, is:
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Net efficiency = Efficiency of **Filling Pipe** − Efficiency of **Emptying Pipe**

Total Capacity (LCM of 12, 21) = 84 units

Efficiency: Filling = 84 ÷ 12 = 7; Emptying = 84 ÷ 21 = 4

Net Efficiency = 7 − 4 = 3 units/hour

Time for **half tank** = (84 ÷ 2) ÷ 3 = 42 ÷ 3 = 14 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 14 hours.**

**__Alternate Method__**

 
 **Pipe Type** **Time (Hours)** **Total Work (LCM)** **Efficiency** 
 Filling Pipe (A) 12 84 +7 
 Emptying Pipe (B) 21 −4 

**Given:** Filling time = 12 hours, Emptying time = 21 hours.

**Formula Used:** Time Taken = Total Work / Combined Efficiency

⇒ Total Capacity of tank = LCM(12, 21) = 84 units

⇒ Combined efficiency of both pipes = 7 − 4 = 3 units/hour

⇒ Target capacity (Half tank) = 84 ÷ 2 = 42 units

⇒ Time taken = 42 ÷ 3 = 14 hours

**∴ The correct answer is 14 hours.**

**__Additional Information__**

Net Work Done

When one pipe fills (rate x) and another empties (rate y), the net rate is (1/x − 1/y) per hour.

Pipes & Cisterns Sign Convention

Inlet pipes contribute **positive efficiency** while outlet (leak) pipes contribute **negative efficiency**.

Capacity vs Time

Time taken is inversely proportional to efficiency for a constant volume.</p

questions.question: Two taps, X and Y, can fill a tank in 12 hours and 24 hours, respectively. If both the taps are open, then due to leakage, it takes 30 minutes more to fill the tank. If the tank is full, how long will it take for the leakage alone to empty the tank?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Net time without leak = (12 × 24) ÷ (12 + 24) = 8 hours.

Net time with leak = 8 hours + 30 minutes = 8.5 hours.

Leak efficiency = (1/8) − (1/8.5) = 0.5 ÷ (8 × 8.5) = 1 ÷ 136.

Time for leak alone = 136 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 136 hr.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

 **Tap/Leak**
 **Time (hr)**

 **Tap X**

Combined efficiency of **X + Y** = 2 + 1 = 3 units/hr.

⇒ Time taken without leak = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 hours.

⇒ Time taken with **Leak (L)** = 8 hr + 30 min = 8.5 hours.

⇒ Combined efficiency (X + Y − L) = 24 ÷ 8.5 = 24 ÷ (17/2) = 48/17 units/hr.

⇒ Leak efficiency (L) = (X + Y efficiency) − (Combined efficiency with leak)

⇒ L = 3 − (48/17) = (51 − 48) ÷ 17 = 3/17 units/hr.

⇒ Time taken by **leak alone** to empty = Total Work ÷ L efficiency

Pipes and Cisterns Concept

Inlet pipes add to the volume (positive efficiency), while outlet pipes or leaks reduce the volume (negative efficiency).

Net Time Formula

If two pipes fill a tank in x and y hours respectively, time taken together is (x × y) ÷ (x + y).

Leakage Effect

A leak reduces the net filling efficiency. If filling takes T₁ hours and with a leak it takes T₂ hours, leak time is (T₁ × T₂) ÷ (T₂ − T₁).</p

questions.question: A pipe can fill a tank in 8 hours. Another pipe can empty the filled tank in 16 hours. If both the pipes are opened simultaneously, then the time (in hours) in which the tank will be three-fourth filled, is:
questions.solution:

Net efficiency = **Filling rate** − **Emptying rate**.

Let **Total capacity** (LCM of 8 and 16) = 16 units.

Filling pipe efficiency = 16 ÷ 8 = 2; Emptying pipe efficiency = 16 ÷ 16 = 1.

Combined efficiency = 2 − 1 = 1 unit/hour.

Time for 3/4 filled = (3/4 × 16) ÷ 1 = 12 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 12 hours.**

**Given:** Filling time = 8 hours, Emptying time = 16 hours.

**Formula Used:** Work = Efficiency × Time; Net Efficiency = (1/Filling time) − (1/Emptying time).

 
 **Pipe Type** **Time (hrs)** **Total Capacity (LCM)** **Efficiency** 
 Filling Pipe 8 16 units +2 
 Emptying Pipe 16 −1 

⇒ **Combined efficiency** of both pipes = 2 − 1 = 1 unit/hour.

⇒ Target volume to be filled = 3/4 × Total Capacity

⇒ Target volume = 3/4 × 16 = 12 units.

⇒ Time taken = Target volume ÷ Combined efficiency

⇒ Time taken = 12 ÷ 1 = 12 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 12 hours.**

Pipes and Cisterns Concept

Filling pipes (inlets) have **positive efficiency**, while emptying pipes (outlets) have **negative efficiency**.

Net Work Formula

If pipe A fills in 'x' hours and pipe B empties in 'y' hours, net work in 1 hour = (1/x − 1/y). If x < y, the tank will eventually fill.

Fractional Filling

To find time for a specific fraction of the tank, multiply the total fill time by that **fractional value**.</p

questions.question: A cistern can be filled with water by a pipe in 10 hours, and it can be emptied by asecond pipe in 8 hours. If both the pipes are opened when the cistern is full, the time in which it will be emptied is:
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__
Time to empty = (**Filling time** × **Emptying time**) ÷ (**Emptying time** − **Filling time**)

Required time = (10 × 8) ÷ (10 − 8)

Required time = 80 ÷ 2 = 40 hours.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

Emptying pipe (B) = 8 hours

**Formula Used:**

Total Work = LCM of individual times

Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time

 **Pipe** **Time (hr)** **Total Capacity (LCM)** **Efficiency (units/hr)**
 A (Filling) 10 40 units +4
 B (Emptying) 8 −5
⇒ Net efficiency of (A + B) = +4 − 5 = −1 unit/hr

⇒ Negative sign indicates the cistern is being emptied.

Inlet and Outlet Pipes

An **Inlet pipe** fills the tank (positive efficiency), while an **Outlet pipe** empties it (negative efficiency).

Net Work Done

Total Work Assumption

questions.question: A and B complete a work in 2 days. If A alone can do it in 38 days, then B alone can do 9-times of the same work in days.
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Combined efficiency of **A + B** = 1/2 work/day

Efficiency of **A** = 1/38 work/day

Efficiency of **B** = 1/2 − 1/38 = (19 − 1)/38 = 18/38 = 9/19 work/day

Time for **B** to do 9-times work = (Total work × 9) ÷ Efficiency of B = 9 ÷ (9/19) = 19 days

**∴ The correct answer is 19 days.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Time taken by **A + B** = 2 days

Time taken by **A** alone = 38 days

**Formula Used:**

Total Work = LCM of time taken

Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time Taken

 
 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 A + B 2 38 19 
 A 38 1 

**Calculations:**

⇒ Efficiency of **B** = Efficiency of (A + B) − Efficiency of A

⇒ Efficiency of **B** = 19 − 1 = 18

⇒ New work to be done = 9 × Total Work = 9 × 38

⇒ Time taken by **B** = (9 × 38) ÷ 18

⇒ Time taken by **B** = 342 ÷ 18 = 19 days

**∴ The correct answer is 19 days.**

**__Additional Information__**

Work and Efficiency Relationship

Efficiency is **inversely proportional** to the time taken to complete a work. If a person completes work in 'n' days, their 1-day work is 1/n.

Combined Work Formula

If A takes 'x' days and B takes 'y' days, together they take (x × y) ÷ (x + y) days to complete the **same work**.</p

questions.question: A tank can be filled by two pipes C and D in 60 minutes and 40 minutes, respectively. How much time will it take to fill the tank from the empty state if D is used for half the time and C and D fill it together for the other half?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Let **Total Capacity** of the tank be 120 units (LCM of 60 and 40).

Efficiency of **Pipe C** = 2 units/min and **Pipe D** = 3 units/min.

Average efficiency for total time T = (Efficiency of D × 0.5) + (Efficiency of C+D × 0.5).

Average efficiency = (3 × 0.5) + (5 × 0.5) = 1.5 + 2.5 = 4 units/min.

Total Time = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 minutes.

**∴ The correct answer is 30 min.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Filling time for **Pipe C** = 60 min, **Pipe D** = 40 min.

 
 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency** 
 Pipe C 60 120 2 
 Pipe D 40 3 

Let the total time taken to fill the tank be **T** minutes.

⇒ Time for which only **Pipe D** works = T/2

⇒ Time for which **Pipes C and D** work together = T/2

⇒ Work done = (Efficiency of D × T/2) + (Efficiency of C+D × T/2) = 120

⇒ (3 × T/2) + ((2 + 3) × T/2) = 120

⇒ 1.5T + 2.5T = 120

⇒ 4T = 120

⇒ T = 30 min

**∴ The correct answer is 30 min.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Pipes and Cisterns Efficiency

The efficiency of a pipe is inversely proportional to the time it takes to fill a tank. Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time.

Combined Pipe Formula

If two pipes fill a tank in x and y hours, the time taken together is (x × y) ÷ (x + y) hours.

Inlet and Outlet Pipes

Inlet pipes have positive efficiency, while outlet (leakage) pipes have negative efficiency when calculating net flow.</p

questions.question: A pipe can fill a tank in 15 hours. Another pipe can empty the filled tank in 40 hours. If both the pipes are opened simultaneously, then the time (in hours) in which the tank will be one-third filled, is:
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Net efficiency = **Filling efficiency** − **Emptying efficiency**.

Let **Total Work** = LCM(15, 40) = 120 units.

Efficiency: Pipe A = +8, Pipe B = −3 → Combined = +5 units/hr.

Required Work = 1/3 × 120 = 40 units.

Time = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 8 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Filling time = 15 hours, Emptying time = 40 hours.

**Formula Used:** Efficiency = Total Work ÷ Time; Time = Work ÷ Efficiency.

 
 **Pipe** **Time (hrs)** **Total Capacity (LCM)** **Efficiency** 
 Filling Pipe 15 120 +8 
 Emptying Pipe 40 −3 

⇒ Net efficiency of both pipes = 8 − 3 = 5 units/hr.

⇒ Capacity to be filled = 1/3 × 120 = 40 units.

⇒ Time required = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 8 hours.**

Pipes and Cisterns Concept

Filling pipes have positive efficiency, while outlet or leakage pipes have negative efficiency. Total capacity is typically assumed as the LCM of individual times.

Net Work Formula

If pipe A fills in x hrs and pipe B empties in y hrs, net work done in 1 hr = (1/x − 1/y). Time to fill completely = (xy)/(y − x).</p

questions.question: There are two pumps to fill a tank with water. The first pump can fill the empty tank in 6 hours, while the second in 8 hours. If both the pumps are opened at the same time and kept open for 2 hours, the part of tank that will be filled up is:
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__
Combined **Efficiency** per hour = 1/6 + 1/8 = (4 + 3)/24 = 7/24

Part filled in **2 hours** = (7/24) × 2 = 7/12

**∴ The correct answer is 7/12.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Time taken by **Pump 1** = 6 hours

Time taken by **Pump 2** = 8 hours

Duration both pumps are open = 2 hours

**Formula Used:**

**Total Work** = LCM of individual times

**Efficiency** = Total Work ÷ Time

**Part filled** = (Total efficiency × Time) ÷ Total Work

 **Person** **Days** **Total Work** **Efficiency**
 Pump 1 6 24 4
 Pump 2 8 3
⇒ Total Efficiency of both pumps = 4 + 3 = 7 units/hour

⇒ Work done in 2 hours = 7 × 2 = 14 units

⇒ Part of tank filled = Work done ÷ Total Work

⇒ Part of tank filled = 14 ÷ 24 = 7/12

**∴ The correct answer is 7/12.**

**__Additional Information__**

Pipes & Cisterns Basics

Filling pipes have **positive efficiency**, while outlet/leakage pipes have **negative efficiency**.

Combined Work Formula

If two pipes fill a tank in x and y hours respectively, they together fill it in (x × y) ÷ (x + y) hours.

Remaining Part

If 7/12 of the tank is filled, the **remaining part** to be filled is 1 − 7/12 = 5/12.</p

questions.question: A pipe can fill a tank in 12 hours. Another pipe can empty the filled tank in 24 hours. If both the pipes are opened simultaneously, then the time (in hours) in which the tank will be two-third filled, is:
questions.solution:
__Shortcut Trick__

Net efficiency = **1/12 − 1/24 = 1/24** units per hour.

Time for full tank = **24 hours**.

Time for 2/3 filled = **24 × 2/3 = 16 hours**.

**∴ The correct answer is 16 hours.**

**__Alternate Method__**

**Given:** Filling Pipe **(A) = 12 hours**, Emptying Pipe **(B) = 24 hours**.

 **Pipe**

 **Efficiency**

 Pipe A (Inlet)
 12
 24 Units

**Calculations:**

⇒ Combined Efficiency of (A + B) = **2 − 1 = 1 unit/hour**.

⇒ Target Work = 2/3 of Total Work = **2/3 × 24 = 16 units**.

⇒ Time taken = Target Work ÷ Combined Efficiency

⇒ Time taken = **16 ÷ 1 = 16 hours**.

**∴ The correct answer is 16 hours.**

**__Additional Information__**

Net Work Done

When one pipe fills and another empties, net work per hour = **1/x − 1/y**, where x is filling time and y is emptying time.

Efficiency Concept

Inlet pipes have **positive efficiency** while outlet (leakage) pipes have **negative efficiency**.

Fractional Work

To find time for a specific fraction of work, multiply the **total time** by that **fraction**.</p
